explain: nDCG divides by the DCG of the ideal ranking built from the qrels. Relevant abstracts outside the pool are no longer known, so the ideal gets smaller and the same BM25 ranking captures a larger fraction of it. The run did not change; the yardstick shrank.

courseTitle: Text embeddings and semantic search
lessonTitle: Lab: train a tiny encoder with in-batch negatives and measure it
question: In the lab, each query in a batch of 256 can be limited to a group of 8 passages instead of all 256. Which statement about that experiment is right?
options: The group-of-8 run sees fewer training pairs, so it is not a fair comparison
Every run uses the same pairs and steps; only the number of negatives per query (7 vs 255) differs
The group-of-8 run has a larger loss, so it must learn faster
Masking changes the positive passage for each query
explain: The mask only hides other passages from each query's softmax, so data, batch, steps and positives stay fixed. That isolates the effect of the negative count, which comparing batch sizes alone cannot do, because a bigger batch also means fewer steps per epoch.

courseTitle: Text embeddings and semantic search
lessonTitle: Chunking documents and adapting a model to your corpus
question: An off-the-shelf model scores nDCG@10 0.40 on your legal corpus, BM25 scores 0.55, and you have no labeled queries. What is the most reasonable next step?
options: Generate synthetic queries for your passages, train GPL-style with cross-encoder pseudo-labels, and compare against BM25 on a small hand-labeled test set
Ship the dense model, since dense retrieval is newer
Fine-tune on MS MARCO again
Lower the similarity threshold until more passages come back
explain: Without labels, synthetic queries over your own corpus are the standard adaptation route (GPL, InPars), and the cross-encoder labels guard against bad queries. You still need a small set of real, held-out queries to tell whether it worked, and BM25 or a hybrid remains the fallback. More general-domain data does not target the domain gap.

courseTitle: Tokenization with Byte Pair Encoding (BPE)
lessonTitle: Training BPE: count adjacent pairs, merge the top one, repeat
question: Starting from the initial corpus, suppose newest appeared 9 times instead of 6 (everything else unchanged). Which pair would be merged first?
options: (e, s), still tied with (s, t) and (t, _) at 12
(l, o), because low is the most frequent word
(w, e), which rises to 11
(n, e), because newest is now the most frequent word
explain: Each of (e, s), (s, t), (t, _) becomes $9 + 3 = 12$, and (w, e) becomes $9 + 2 = 11$. The top count is a three-way tie at 12, and the first-seen rule picks (e, s). Word frequency alone does not decide: (l, o) gets 7 and (n, e) gets 9.

courseTitle: Tokenization with Byte Pair Encoding (BPE)
lessonTitle: Special tokens, chat templates and prompt boundaries
question: A service builds each prompt as system_text + user_text and encodes it with `enc.encode(prompt, allowed_special="all")`. What is wrong?
options: Nothing; allowed_special only changes how decoding works
It is slower, but the ids are identical either way
It raises ValueError on every prompt
A user who types a special string such as <|endoftext|> gets the real control token, so their text can end the document or fake structure the model trusts
explain: allowed_special="all" turns every special string in the text into its control id, including strings typed by users. Allow special tokens only in text you wrote, and encode user text with the defaults (which raise) or with disallowed_special=() so it stays plain text.

courseTitle: Training deep nets in practice: init, optimizers, schedules, debugging
lessonTitle: Initialization: keeping signals alive through 30 layers
question: Why does He initialization use 2 / fan-in rather than Xavier's 1 / fan-in (equal fans) for ReLU layers?
options: ReLU doubles the gradient on the positive side
The factor 2 accounts for the bias term
ReLU zeroes about half of a symmetric pre-activation, halving the mean square, and the factor 2 cancels that
Larger weights train faster, so 2 is a safe speed-up
explain: With zero-mean symmetric pre-activations, ReLU keeps only the positive half, so the average of $\mathrm{relu}(z)^2$ is $\mathrm{Var}(z)/2$. Multiplying Var(w) by 2 restores a per-layer factor of exactly 1.

courseTitle: Training deep nets in practice: init, optimizers, schedules, debugging
lessonTitle: Mixed precision: fp16, bf16 and loss scaling
question: Your gradients include many values around 1e-9 and you want to avoid a loss scaler. Which format works, and what does it give up?
options: fp16, because subnormals reach down past 1e-9
bf16: fp32's exponent range keeps 1e-9 representable, at the cost of only 7 mantissa bits (spacing 0.0078 near 1)
fp16, because it has more mantissa bits than bf16
Either one: both have 8 exponent bits
explain: fp16's smallest positive number is 2^-24, about 6e-8, so 1e-9 rounds to 0 unless the loss is scaled. bf16 keeps fp32's 8 exponent bits, so range is not the problem; precision is, which is why the weights stay in fp32.

courseTitle: Training deep nets in practice: init, optimizers, schedules, debugging
lessonTitle: Instrumenting a run: gradient norms, update ratios, activation stats
question: A run's loss sits at 2.30 (10 classes) for 300 steps. Every layer's update-to-weight ratio is about 1e-8, and the activation std drops about 8x per layer. Most likely cause?
options: Weights initialized far too small, so the signal and gradients vanish
A learning rate 30x too high
model.eval() was never called
Dropout is too strong
explain: A constant ln 10 loss means the network predicts uniformly. The per-layer scale collapse matches lesson 1's analysis of a too-small init, and ratios of 1e-8 mean the weights are effectively frozen. A too-high rate gives large ratios and climbing gradient norms instead.

courseTitle: Vector search and ANN: HNSW, IVF, PQ and production indexes
lessonTitle: HNSW layers: a skip list made of graphs
question: A teammate sets m_L very high (for example 5) so the hierarchy is taller. What does the HNSW paper say happens when m_L is too large?
options: Recall drops to zero because layer 0 becomes empty
Memory shrinks because fewer links are stored
Neighbors overlap more across layers, so extra layers add little and search gets slower
Nothing changes; m_L only affects build time
explain: The paper explains that larger m_L means more overlap between layers (more nodes repeated on many layers), which hurts performance, while too small m_L increases the number of hops on each layer. That tradeoff is why it picks m_L = 1/ln M, matching a skip list with p = 1/M.

courseTitle: Vector search and ANN: HNSW, IVF, PQ and production indexes
lessonTitle: Production scale: disk, rescoring, filters and updates
question: A query with a selective filter (1 percent of rows match) returns 0 or 1 results from an HNSW index with ef_search = 40. Which explanation fits?
options: The graph is disconnected, so the filtered rows are unreachable
The index post-filters about 40 candidates, so about 0.4 match on average
Cosine distance cannot be combined with WHERE clauses
ef_search is ignored when a filter is present
explain: With post-filtering, expected matches = candidates times selectivity = 40 x 0.01 = 0.4. Raise ef_search, enable iterative scans, or use a separate index or partition for that filter.

courseTitle: Software supply chain security
lessonTitle: Typosquatting and dependency confusion: winning by name
question: Why does moving internal packages under an npm scope such as @acme defeat dependency confusion?
options: npm refuses to publish scoped packages publicly
A scope maps to exactly one registry, so the resolver never asks the public registry for @acme packages
Scoped names are encrypted
Scoped packages cannot have install scripts
explain: npm's documentation: scopes have a many-to-one relationship with registries; a scope only ever points to one registry. The public registry is simply not consulted for that name. (Also claim the @acme scope publicly so nobody else can.)

courseTitle: Software supply chain security
lessonTitle: CI secrets: Codecov and the keys inside every pipeline
question: Codecov's attacker never touched Codecov's git repository. Why didn't that protect anyone?
options: The attacker deleted the repository
Customers downloaded the script from a storage bucket at run time, so the bucket was the real source of truth
GitHub was also compromised
Git repositories cannot store shell scripts
explain: What runs is what is downloaded, not what is in git. The customer who compared the downloaded script with the published hash checked the right thing.

courseTitle: Software supply chain security
lessonTitle: Provenance and SLSA levels: a signed record of how it was built
question: Which attack does SLSA Build L3 provenance NOT protect against?
options: A compromised build step forging the provenance
Modifying an artifact after the build
Uploading a locally built package by hand
A maintainer committing a backdoor to the main branch, which is then built normally
explain: The build was faithful to the source; the source was bad. That needs the Source track (enforced review) and human scrutiny, which is exactly the xz problem.

courseTitle: Software supply chain security
lessonTitle: xz-utils II: where the payload hid and how it was caught
question: Which distribution practice would have kept the backdoor out of a package even if the 5.6.1 version was adopted?
options: Verifying the maintainer's signature on the tarball
Running the package's test suite
Building the package from the tagged git source instead of the release tarball
Using a newer compiler
explain: The trigger lived only in the tarball. Arch Linux switched xz to build from git when the backdoor was disclosed. The signature was valid (Jia Tan signed it), and the tests passed.

courseTitle: Synthetic data and model collapse
lessonTitle: Reproduce collapse yourself: simulate the loops, measure diversity
question: Over five rounds of a synthetic data loop, distinct-2 of the generated set stays near 0.7, but coverage of the rare slice of a held-out real set falls from 0.5 to 0.2. What is the best reading?
options: The generator is fine: distinct-2 is stable, so diversity is preserved
The held-out real set is too small to trust, so ignore it
Diversity is improving, because rare-slice coverage is supposed to fall as quality rises
The phrasing stays varied but rare content is disappearing: the early-collapse signature of losing the tails
explain: distinct-n measures variety inside the generated set, not whether it still covers the real distribution. Falling rare-slice coverage is exactly the tail loss of lessons 1 and 3, which internal metrics can miss.

courseTitle: Synthetic data and model collapse
lessonTitle: Synthetic data at scale: rephrasing, textbooks, reward-filtered SFT
question: A synthetic textbook includes a reworded version of a test question from MMLU (Massive Multitask Language Understanding, a 57-subject benchmark). Your decontamination uses 10-gram overlap followed by a SequenceMatcher check. What happens, and what is the sturdier defense?
options: It is caught, because SequenceMatcher compares every sample with every benchmark item
It is caught, because rewording keeps most 10-word runs intact
It does not matter, since contamination only affects pretraining data, not synthetic data
It slips through, since no 10-word run is shared; keep a protected in-house evaluation set the generator never saw
explain: The 10-gram step decides which samples are compared at all, so a paraphrase with no shared 10-gram is never checked. Liu et al. note exactly this gap and recommend safeguarded private benchmarks.

courseTitle: System calls and mmap
lessonTitle: Editing the map: munmap, mprotect, mremap and how exec builds it
question: A program grows a 1 GiB mapping with mremap(p, 1 GiB, 2 GiB, MREMAP_MAYMOVE) and keeps using a pointer it saved earlier, q = p + 4096. What can go wrong?
options: Nothing: mremap always grows a mapping in place
If the kernel moved the mapping, q points into the old, now unmapped range, so using it can fault
The first 1 GiB is copied byte by byte, so q sees stale data
mremap fails because MREMAP_MAYMOVE only works on file mappings
explain: With MREMAP_MAYMOVE the kernel may relocate the mapping when there is no room to grow in place, and mremap(2) warns that absolute pointers into the old location become invalid. Use the returned address, or store offsets from the start instead of raw pointers.

courseTitle: System calls and mmap
lessonTitle: When mmap wins, when it hurts, and how to steer it
question: Eight worker processes each need read-only access to the same 2 GiB lookup table on a machine with 64 GiB of RAM. Which approach uses the least memory?
options: Each worker mmaps the file with PROT_READ
Each worker reads the file into its own malloc buffer
Each worker mmaps with MAP_ANONYMOUS and copies the file in
One worker reads it and sends it to the others over a pipe
explain: Read-only file mappings in all eight workers point at the same page cache pages, so the table occupies about 2 GiB once. Reading into private buffers keeps eight copies (16 GiB) plus the page cache copy. Anonymous memory is private per process too. This read-mostly, fits-in-RAM, shared case is where mmap clearly wins.

courseTitle: Tail latency (p99, p99.9) and coordinated omission
lessonTitle: Taming the tail: hedged requests and honest reporting
question: A colleague says: 'Our load test with wrk2 at 5,000 requests per second shows p99 = 900 ms but production p99 at the same traffic is 20 ms, so wrk2 must be broken.' What is the most likely explanation to check first?
options: HdrHistogram rounds values up by 45x
Production percentiles are always lower than test percentiles
wrk2 sends requests twice
wrk2 measures from intended send times, so if the server cannot sustain 5,000 req/s, queueing builds up and is honestly reported; check that the achieved rate matched the target
explain: If the requested rate exceeds what the system can serve, the backlog grows during the run and every request's latency since its intended time keeps rising. Compare the reported Requests/sec to the -R target and check the test setup (for example, one client machine as bottleneck) before blaming the tool.

courseTitle: Telecom and satellite security: SS7, SIM swapping, 5G and space links
lessonTitle: Diameter in 4G roaming: the same trust model on IP
question: Your edge sees an Update-Location-Request about IMSI 208010000000042 arriving from a partner realm. Your network is 234-15. What should a category-style rule conclude?
options: Accept: ULRs from partners are always fine
Accept, but only if the subscriber is a VIP
Reject: your HSS is not that subscriber's home, so a ULR for them should not be sent to you
Reject: ULRs are category 1 and never cross networks
explain: A visited MME sends Update-Location to the subscriber's home HSS. IMSI 20801... belongs to network 208-01, not you, so a ULR for it addressed to your HSS has no legitimate purpose. ULRs do cross networks, so they are not category 1.

courseTitle: Telecom and satellite security: SS7, SIM swapping, 5G and space links
lessonTitle: Inside the 5G core: service APIs, OAuth tokens, SEPP and slices
question: An AMF presents a valid NRF-signed token with scope nudm-sdm, and calls a UDM operation that needs nudm-uecm. What should the UDM return?
options: 403: the token is genuine but does not grant this service
200 OK: any signed token is enough
401: the signature is invalid
It should ask the NRF to widen the scope automatically
explain: Authentication (valid signature) and authorisation (the scope covers this service) are separate checks; TS 33.501 13.4.1 puts the allowed services in the scope claim.

courseTitle: Telecom and satellite security: SS7, SIM swapping, 5G and space links
lessonTitle: Salt Typhoon: espionage inside carrier networks (2024 to 2025)
question: A router's running config shows the TACACS+ server changed to an address outside your management network. What is the most important concern?
options: The router will boot slower
Administrator logins may now be sent to an attacker, who can capture credentials
SNMP will stop working
The router's clock will drift
explain: AA25-239A reports actors redirecting TACACS+ to their own infrastructure to capture authentication attempts. Treat it as a credential compromise: revert from the golden config, rotate the TACACS+ secret and admin credentials, and hunt for other changes.

courseTitle: Telecom and satellite security: SS7, SIM swapping, 5G and space links
lessonTitle: Detecting GNSS spoofing, and authenticated navigation signals
question: What does Galileo OSNMA, as operational in 2025, authenticate?
options: The Galileo open-service navigation data (ephemeris and timing parameters), so receivers can verify it came from Galileo unmodified
Every receiver's position
The exact arrival time of every signal at pseudorange level
GPS signals only
explain: OSNMA signs I/NAV navigation data on E1-B. EUSPA says pseudorange-level protection will come from the planned Signal Authentication Service, and GPS L1 C/A data authentication is a future evolution.

courseTitle: Temporal reasoning: years of experience and current roles
lessonTitle: Allen relations, current roles and time-scoped queries
question: At month granularity with half-open intervals, role X is Jan 2020 to Jun 2020 and role Y is Jul 2020 to Dec 2020 (both as written, inclusive). Which Allen relation holds for X relative to Y?
options: before, because June is before July
overlaps, because they share the month boundary
during
meets
explain: As half-open intervals X is [2020-01, 2020-07) and Y is [2020-07, 2021-01). X's exclusive end equals Y's start, which is the definition of meets: back-to-back, no gap and no overlap.

courseTitle: Test-time compute scaling: sampling, search and thinking longer
lessonTitle: Precision: majority vote, best-of-N and when they plateau
question: Your majority-vote accuracy on a math benchmark stops improving between N = 64 and N = 512, but pass@512 (checked against the answer key) keeps rising. What is the most likely reason?
options: Samples become correlated at large N
On the unsolved problems the correct answer is a minority answer, so adding votes reinforces the wrong mode
The model runs out of context window
pass@k is computed incorrectly at large N
explain: Majority vote converges to the mode of the answer distribution. For problems where a wrong answer is the mode, more samples raise coverage but not voting accuracy. That is the plateau Brown et al. report.

courseTitle: Test-time compute scaling: sampling, search and thinking longer
lessonTitle: Thinking longer: reasoning models and budget forcing
question: DeepSeek-R1-Zero's responses became much longer during RL even though no reward term asked for length. Why is that evidence for test-time scaling?
options: Longer outputs are always rewarded by GRPO
Length was capped at 1,000 tokens
The model copied long human traces
The reward was only for correctness and format, so the model discovered that spending more tokens per problem raised its success rate
explain: R1-Zero's rewards were rule-based accuracy and format rewards. Growth in thinking length alongside accuracy shows the policy learned to buy correctness with test-time tokens.

courseTitle: Test-time training and learned memory: TTT layers and Titans
lessonTitle: A hidden state that is itself a model you train while reading
question: Which of these changes the trained weights of a network itself at inference, instead of a per-sequence state that starts fresh for every input?
options: A TTT-Linear layer reading a 10,000-token prompt
Linear attention accumulating v k-transpose over a document
LaCT updating its SwiGLU fast weights once per 2048-token chunk
Sun et al. (2019): one rotation-prediction gradient step on each test image before classifying it
explain: Sun et al. update the classifier's own shared parameters with a self-supervised loss on the test image. The other three are fast weights: a TTT layer's W, linear attention's state and LaCT's fast weights all start from a learned or zero initial value for each sequence and are thrown away afterwards, while the network's ordinary weights stay frozen.

courseTitle: Test-time training and learned memory: TTT layers and Titans
lessonTitle: Titans' three architectures, worked one segment at a time
question: In MAC, why does segment 3's attention not see the memory update made from segment 3's own tokens?
options: Because the memory is read before the segment is written: h comes from M_2, and the write that adds segment 3 happens after attention
Because MAC never writes segment tokens into the memory
Because persistent tokens block the memory during segment 3
Because the memory is only updated at the end of the sequence
explain: MAC's order is retrieve, attend, write, gate. Retrieval reads M_(t-1), from before the segment, so attention combines the compressed past with the exact current segment. Only the final gate reads the freshly written M_t.

courseTitle: Thread caches and magazines
lessonTitle: One lock, many cores: why a shared slab cache stops scaling
question: A service spends 50 ns per malloc inside a global allocator lock. Ignoring everything else, what is the most mallocs per second the whole machine can do through that lock?
options: 20 million per second, regardless of core count
20 million per second per core
It depends only on how fast each core runs application code
Unlimited, since a mutex costs nothing when uncontended
explain: One holder at a time, 50 ns each: $1/(50 \text{ ns}) = 2 \times 10^7$ per second for the whole machine. More cores add waiters, not throughput.

courseTitle: Thread caches and magazines
lessonTitle: Today: thread caches, per-CPU caches and restartable sequences
question: An application runs 4,000 threads on a 32-CPU machine, most of them blocked most of the time. Which allocator front-end is the better fit for memory footprint, and why?
options: Per-thread caches, because blocked threads release their caches automatically
Per-CPU caches, because the number of caches is bounded by the 32 CPUs rather than the 4,000 threads
Neither: a global lock is best when threads are mostly blocked
Per-thread caches, because rseq does not work with more threads than CPUs
explain: Per-thread caches keep idle objects in every thread's cache, including the thousands of sleeping ones, or must shrink each cache until it is useless. Per-CPU caches exist only per logical CPU, so at most 32 hold memory, and the running threads share them.

courseTitle: Threat hunting
lessonTitle: Stacking: let the rare thing rise to the top
question: You stack 'process opened a handle to LSASS' across 3,000 machines. One backup agent made 50,000 such events, all on a single server, so sorted by count() it looks like the most common program. Which aggregation shows it is present on only one machine?
options: Sorting by time instead of by count
dcount(DeviceId) per process, the number of distinct devices
count() of events per process
sum of event sizes per process
explain: Counting distinct devices measures prevalence: a value seen on one device stays at 1 however many events that device produces, so the backup agent rises into the rare list next to the other one-machine programs, where a person can confirm it is the expected server. Counting raw events lets any chatty process look 'common' and sink out of a least-frequent list.

courseTitle: Threat hunting
lessonTitle: An intelligence-driven hunt: living off the land and Volt Typhoon
question: A Volt Typhoon-style actor copied ntds.dit with ntdsutil and then deleted the copy. Which evidence from the hunt plan most likely still records where the copy was written?
options: Event 1102
ESENT events 216, 325, 326 and 327 in the Application log
The PortProxy registry key
The firewall log
explain: AA23-144A notes that the ESENT events' details should contain the file path where the copies were created, and that this 'can greatly aid in a hunt operation' because the files themselves can be deleted. Event 1102 would only show that a log was cleared, and the port proxy and firewall evidence concern a different behaviour.

courseTitle: Threat hunting
lessonTitle: Measuring a hunt programme, and where to practise
question: A hunt team spends a month hunting for encoded PowerShell, which already has a tested production rule that fires reliably. What does TaHiTI suggest they should have done first?
options: Checked the state of existing detections to avoid hunting for activity that traditional detection already covers
Hunted only for file hashes
Nothing; repeating hunts is always good
Bought a new EDR
explain: TaHiTI says continuous insight into the state of detection mechanisms is required 'to avoid hunting for malicious activity that is already covered'. Hunting time is scarce; spend it where the coverage map is empty or untested.

courseTitle: Cyber threat intelligence
lessonTitle: Collection: where intelligence comes from, and what it is worth
question: Your SOC confirmed 40 malicious domains last quarter. A paid feed of 2 million domains contained 12 of them, all also present in your free ISAC feed. What does this measurement show?
options: The paid feed is the most valuable because it is the largest
The paid feed added no unique detections against what you saw last quarter; check whether it serves another requirement before renewing
The ISAC feed must be wrong because it is smaller
Both feeds should be dropped because neither had all 40
explain: Unique contribution was zero against confirmed activity, so the feed's value, if any, lies elsewhere (another PIR, earlier delivery, or threats you have not yet seen). Size says nothing about relevance, and no feed will contain everything, so missing some confirmed domains is expected.

courseTitle: Cyber threat intelligence
lessonTitle: Kill chain and ATT&CK as analytic frames
question: A 2024 advisory tags log clearing as T1070.001. Your 2026 detection list (ATT&CK v20) has a rule tagged T1685.005. What is the right conclusion?
options: They are unrelated techniques
They describe the same behaviour under different ATT&CK versions; translate the ID before measuring coverage
The advisory is wrong
T1685.005 must be deprecated
explain: In ATT&CK v20, T1070.001 Clear Windows Event Logs redirects to T1685.005 under Disable or Modify Tools. Mappings are version-specific, so compare like with like.

courseTitle: Cyber threat intelligence
lessonTitle: Attribution: levels, evidence and its limits
question: In April 2021 the US named the SVR; in April 2022 Mandiant merged UNC2452 into APT29. Why might a vendor take a year longer than a government?
options: Vendors are not allowed to attribute
The vendor only reached the conclusion once its own firsthand evidence supported it, while the government could draw on intelligence sources a company does not have
The government statement was wrong
APT29 did not exist before 2022
explain: Mandiant said its merge was 'based on firsthand data gathered by Mandiant'. Governments can use signals and human intelligence that are not public, which supports the sponsor rung earlier but cannot be checked by outsiders.

courseTitle: Thinking like an attacker: threat models and security principles
lessonTitle: Assets and adversaries: what is worth taking, and by whom
question: Your adversary list contains only 'anonymous internet attacker'. What does the model most likely miss?
options: Denial-of-service attacks
Attacks on the encryption of web traffic
Phishing emails
Misuse by people who already have legitimate access
explain: Insiders start inside the trust boundary with real credentials. Anonymous internet attackers can attempt denial of service, phishing and network attacks, so those are not the gap.

courseTitle: Thinking like an attacker: threat models and security principles
lessonTitle: Attack trees: start from the attacker's goal
question: You can spend money on one defence. Which helps the root of an attack tree most?
options: Raising the cost of the branch that is currently cheapest
Raising the cost of the most expensive branch
Adding a new leaf to every branch
Whichever defence is cheapest to buy
explain: The root of an OR tree equals its cheapest branch. Raising any other branch leaves the root unchanged. Price matters, but only after you know which branch it changes.

courseTitle: Thinking like an attacker: threat models and security principles
lessonTitle: Case: Target 2013, a vendor login across a trust boundary
question: FireEye raised alerts on 30 November and 2 December, yet data kept leaving until mid-December. What does this teach about defence in depth?
options: A detection layer only counts if someone acts on it: detection without response is not a working layer
FireEye was the wrong product
Detection is useless against skilled attackers
Alerts should be turned off to reduce noise
explain: The signal was there. The response process failed. The next lesson shows why layers that share a failure, such as one ignored alert queue, add less protection than they appear to.

courseTitle: Tiered memory: placing pages across DRAM, CXL and SSD
lessonTitle: How Linux ranks nodes into tiers: abstract distance
question: A CXL device is onlined through the dax kmem driver, but firmware provides no HMAT or CDAT performance data. Which tier does its node join?
options: memory_tier4, the same tier as DRAM, so it is never a demotion target
memory_tier22, from the kmem default adistance of 5 x 576 = 2880
The slowest possible tier, because it has no CPUs
None: the kernel refuses to online memory without performance data
explain: drivers/dax/kmem.c starts from MEMTIER_DEFAULT_DAX_ADISTANCE (5 x 576 = 2880) and only overrides it if a performance-based algorithm can compute one. 2880 / 128 = 22.5, so tier 22. Memory onlined as ordinary system RAM instead defaults to 576 and would share tier 4 with DRAM.

courseTitle: Time-series forecasting: baselines, smoothing and honest backtests
lessonTitle: Naive, seasonal naive and simple exponential smoothing
question: On the test year, seasonal naive has MAE 24.25 and naive has MAE 37.92. What would most directly remove seasonal naive's remaining error on this series?
options: Use a smaller alpha
Switch from MAE to RMSE
Use only the last 12 months of training data
Add a trend term, since all its errors are positive by roughly one year of growth
explain: Every seasonal naive error is positive, between 19 and 30, close to 12 months x 2 per month = 24. That is a systematic bias from ignoring the trend. A method with both trend and season terms (Holt-Winters, next lesson) addresses it. Changing the metric changes the score, not the forecast.

courseTitle: TLS and PKI in practice
lessonTitle: The TLS 1.3 handshake, message by message
question: Which handshake messages in TLS 1.3 can a passive observer read in plaintext?
options: ClientHello, ServerHello and Certificate
Only ClientHello and ServerHello
None; everything is encrypted from the first byte
All of them; only application data is encrypted
explain: RFC 9846 encrypts every handshake message after ServerHello. The two Hello messages must be in clear because the keys do not exist until both key shares have been exchanged.

courseTitle: TLS and PKI in practice
lessonTitle: Downgrade attacks: POODLE, BEAST, Logjam and the fixes
question: A server supports TLS 1.2 and SSL 3.0 and implements TLS_FALLBACK_SCSV. Interference on the path causes a browser to fall back and retry with SSL 3.0. What happens?
options: The server accepts SSL 3.0, because the client asked for it
The browser detects the attacker's TCP reset and alerts the user
The server silently upgrades the connection to TLS 1.2
The server sees the SCSV, knows it supports a higher version than offered, and aborts with inappropriate_fallback
explain: The SCSV tells the server "this is a fallback retry". If the server could have done better, a fallback means someone interfered, so it refuses.

courseTitle: TLS and PKI in practice
lessonTitle: Certificate authorities, the CA/Browser Forum and ACME
question: An attacker briefly hijacks example.com's DNS records at the registrar. What can they most likely do?
options: Obtain a valid DV certificate for example.com via a DNS or HTTP challenge, since they now control the name
Nothing, because certificates require company paperwork
Only read existing traffic
Revoke example.com's current certificate
explain: DV issuance trusts whoever controls the domain at validation time. CAA does not help if the attacker can also change the CAA record. CT monitoring is how the real owner finds out (lesson 12).

courseTitle: TLS and PKI in practice
lessonTitle: HSTS, preloading and why key pinning fell out of favour
question: A site sends HSTS with max-age of one year. A user who visited last week is now on a malicious Wi-Fi and types `site.example`. What happens?
options: The first request goes out over HTTP and can be stripped
The browser upgrades to HTTPS internally before sending anything, so there is no plain request to strip
The browser asks the user whether to use HTTPS
HSTS does not apply to typed URLs
explain: The stored policy makes the browser rewrite the scheme itself. The remaining gap is a user who has never visited (or whose policy expired), which preloading closes.

courseTitle: TLS and PKI in practice
lessonTitle: Post-quantum key exchange: ML-KEM hybrids in TLS
question: Why does TLS use a hybrid (X25519 plus ML-KEM) instead of ML-KEM alone?
options: ML-KEM cannot produce a 32-byte secret
Because X25519 is quantum-safe
So the connection stays secure if either algorithm holds: against quantum attackers via ML-KEM, and against a future classical break of the young ML-KEM via X25519
To make the ClientHello smaller
explain: Hybrids hedge both risks. The combined secret feeds the key schedule, so an attacker must break both components to recover the keys.

courseTitle: Triton kernels: block-level GPU programming
lessonTitle: Tiled matmul: 2D pointer blocks, tl.dot and grouped ordering
question: In the grouped-ordering code, what ordering do you get with GROUP_SIZE_M = 1?
options: Column-major: tiles go down each column of C first
Plain row-major: pid_m = pid // num_pid_n and pid_n = pid % num_pid_n
A random permutation of tiles
Every program computes tile (0, 0)
explain: With G = 1, num_pid_in_group = num_pid_n, so group_id = pid // num_pid_n becomes pid_m and pid_n = pid % num_pid_n. Each group is one full row of tiles: exactly row-major order.

courseTitle: Unified multimodal models: one transformer that reads and draws
lessonTitle: Attention masks for mixed text and image sequences
question: A colleague changes the mask so the text token 'cube' (before BOI) can attend to p1 to p4 during training. What goes wrong?
options: Nothing, more attention is always better
Information leaks: training uses image content that will not exist when 'cube' is generated, so train and inference disagree
The model runs out of memory
The image patches can no longer see the text
explain: At inference the caption comes before the image, so when 'cube' is produced there are no patches yet. A mask that lets 'cube' read them teaches the model to rely on information it will never have. The fix is to keep the rows before BOI strictly causal.

courseTitle: Unikernels: one application, one address space, one VM image
lessonTitle: Syscalls become function calls: one address space, one privilege level
question: A team runs an unmodified Linux nginx binary on a unikernel through its binary compatibility layer and sees less gain than the papers report. What is the most likely reason?
options: Binary compatibility disables the hypervisor's virtio drivers
nginx needs fork, which unikernels emulate with slow VM cloning
The binary is compiled for user mode and cannot run in kernel mode
Each syscall instruction still has to be trapped and translated, which costs far more than a direct function call
explain: The unmodified binary still executes syscall instructions, which the unikernel must catch and dispatch: 84 cycles versus 4 for a direct call in Unikraft's measurement. Linking the application against musl and the syscall shim turns those into direct calls.

courseTitle: Unikernels: one application, one address space, one VM image
lessonTitle: Paravirtual I/O up close: one packet through a virtqueue
question: Why does a unikernel coded against uknetdev in polling mode handle millions of packets per second where an interrupt-per-packet design does not?
options: It checks the ring in a loop and moves packets in bursts, so it pays no interrupt or notification per packet
Polling makes each descriptor smaller
Polling lets the guest write directly to the physical network card
Polling disables the hypervisor's isolation
explain: The ring itself is just memory. Per-packet costs come from notifications: interrupts into the guest and kicks out of it. Polling and burst APIs remove them from the hot path, at the price of a core that spins.

courseTitle: Unikernels: one application, one address space, one VM image
lessonTitle: The spectrum: Linux-based unikernels, microVMs and sandboxes
question: Which property does UKL keep that a MirageOS unikernel gives up?
options: A single address space for the application and kernel
Multi-core execution and other processes running beside the linked application
Running the application at supervisor privilege
Static linking of the application with the kernel
explain: UKL links one application into Linux at supervisor privilege, like a unikernel, but keeps Linux's SMP support and lets ordinary processes run beside it. Mirage runs one vCPU and one program per VM.

courseTitle: Vector database internals: SIMD kernels, segments and disk
lessonTitle: Durability and memory tiers: WAL, mmap and disk-based ANN
question: Your 768-d fp32 index needs 31 GB and the machine has 16 GB for page cache. Which change most directly attacks the latency cliff?
options: Switch the vectors to the cached tier so they are pre-loaded at startup
Use a faster SIMD instruction set
Increase the number of segments
Compress the vectors (for example to int8 or PQ codes) so the navigation data fits in RAM, and re-rank with full vectors
explain: Pre-loading cannot fit 31 GB into 16 GB, and SIMD speed is irrelevant when waiting on the SSD. Shrinking what the search touches per hop, and reading exact vectors only for the final re-rank, is exactly the DiskANN-style pattern.

courseTitle: verl: the HybridFlow RL training stack for LLMs
lessonTitle: One GRPO step through the V1 trainer, call by call
question: You halve actor.ppo_micro_batch_size_per_gpu to fix an out-of-memory error. What happens to the learning dynamics?
options: Nothing in principle: micro-batches only split each mini-batch into smaller forward and backward passes with gradient accumulation
Each optimizer step now sees half as many responses
The number of optimizer steps per RL step doubles
GRPO groups get split across micro-batches, which corrupts the advantages
explain: Micro-batching is like gradient accumulation: it trades speed for memory. The mini-batch size, which sets samples per optimizer step, is unchanged. Advantages were already computed on the controller before update_actor, so splitting groups across micro-batches does not affect them.

courseTitle: verl: the HybridFlow RL training stack for LLMs
lessonTitle: Agent loops: multi-turn rollouts and tool calling in verl
question: Why does verl's response_mask put 0 on tool-output tokens?
options: The tool output is too long to fit in the context
Tool tokens have no log-probs, so the KL term would be undefined
The policy did not choose them; training on them would teach the model to predict tool output and misassign credit, so they stay as context only
vLLM cannot generate tool tokens
explain: Tool tokens are observations, like the prompt. They must stay in the sequence because later model tokens depend on them, but their loss weight is 0. verl's estimators multiply advantages by response_mask, and the loss averages only over mask-1 tokens.

courseTitle: Video-LLMs with long-video memory
lessonTitle: Which frames to look at: uniform sampling and the needle problem
question: Why is question-aware keyframe selection awkward for a chat assistant that answers many follow-up questions about the same video?
options: Keyframes are only defined for videos under one minute
Keyframe selection cannot run on GPUs
Keyframes always contain fewer tokens than uniform frames
The selected frames depend on the question, so each new question may need a new selection pass and new visual tokens
explain: Relevance is computed against the prompt. A follow-up about a different moment needs different frames, so the encoding and prefill work is redone instead of reusing one cached representation of the video.

courseTitle: Video world models: Genie, latent actions and neural game engines
lessonTitle: World models, and why Genie learns one from unlabelled video
question: What does Genie learn from that a text-to-video model does not need, and what does it not need that classic world models do?
options: It needs only video, yet offers frame-by-frame control that video models lack
It needs action labels but not text, like classic world models
It needs text captions per frame instead of actions
It needs a hand-written game engine to generate training data
explain: Genie trains on unlabelled video only. Classic world models (Ha and Schmidhuber, Dreamer) need the action at each step; text-to-video models give control only at the level of the whole clip. Genie's latent actions give per-frame control without labels.

courseTitle: Video world models: Genie, latent actions and neural game engines
lessonTitle: Rollout drift and diffusion game engines
question: In DIAMOND's Boxing experiments, one denoising step gave a blurry opponent but three steps gave a crisp one. Why?
options: One step is not enough compute to render any sprite
The opponent's moves are uncertain, so a single step averages possible futures; iterating commits to one mode
The agent's own player is also blurry for the same reason
Blur is caused by the auto-encoder, not the denoiser
explain: A one-step denoiser trained with an L2 loss (mean squared error) outputs the mean of all plausible next frames, which blurs when the future is multimodal, with several distinct likely outcomes (modes). The agent's own player stayed sharp because its action is known to the model. Multi-step sampling drives the sample toward one mode.

courseTitle: Virtualization and hypervisor security
lessonTitle: I/O virtualization: emulation, virtio, passthrough and the IOMMU
question: A host assigns two functions of the same multi-function NIC to two different tenants' VMs. The IOMMU is on. What does the VFIO documentation warn about?
options: Nothing: the IOMMU translates each function separately
Multi-function devices cannot do DMA
Interrupt remapping must be turned off for multi-function devices
Functions inside one enclosure may talk to each other without their traffic reaching the IOMMU, so they belong to one group and should go to one owner
explain: VFIO's documentation names this case: 'a multi-function PCI device with backdoors between functions'. The IOMMU group is the unit of ownership; splitting a group across tenants breaks isolation the IOMMU cannot see.

courseTitle: Virtualization and hypervisor security
lessonTitle: Case: VENOM, the floppy controller every guest had
question: Why were hosts vulnerable to VENOM even when no VM had a virtual floppy disk configured?
options: QEMU initialised the floppy controller for every x86 guest regardless of configuration, so its I/O ports were always reachable
The floppy driver was loaded in the host kernel
Guests could hot-plug a floppy drive themselves
The exploit used the CD-ROM controller instead
explain: Per Red Hat, the FDC was initialised for every x86 and x86_64 guest and could not be removed or disabled. The attack surface was the controller's register interface, not a disk image.

courseTitle: Virtualization and hypervisor security
lessonTitle: The management plane: ESXiArgs, SLP and locking down hosts
question: An admin enables strict lockdown mode on every host, with no exception users and SSH disabled, and vCenter then fails. What happens, per Broadcom's KB?
options: Hosts fall back to normal lockdown automatically
The DCUI still allows root to log in
Nothing; strict mode only affects the web client
The hosts become unmanageable until vCenter is restored; if it cannot be, reinstalling ESXi may be required
explain: Strict mode stops the DCUI. Without exception users and SSH or Shell enabled, losing vCenter leaves no way in, and the KB says a reinstall may be required. Plan break-glass access before turning it on.

courseTitle: Virtualization and hypervisor security
lessonTitle: A defender's playbook for virtualization, and where to practise
question: Which single change most reduces the impact of the next VENOM-style device bug on a KVM host?
options: Raising the guest's RAM
Turning off EPT
Running QEMU unprivileged and confined (SELinux/AppArmor, seccomp), with only the devices each VM needs
Using larger pages for guest memory
explain: VENOM's impact was 'the privileges of the host's QEMU process'. Fewer devices shrink the chance of a bug; a confined, unprivileged QEMU shrinks what a bug gives. EPT and page size do not touch device emulation.

courseTitle: Fine-tuning a vision model (ViT)
lessonTitle: Linear probe, LoRA or full fine-tune: choosing what to train
question: A hospital fine-tunes an ImageNet-21k ViT on 3,000 X-rays from scanner A; it will be deployed on scanner B, which produces visibly different images. Which plan best matches the evidence in this lesson?
options: Full fine-tune with a randomly initialized head, since it has the highest in-distribution accuracy
Train only the position embeddings
LP-FT: fit the head on frozen features first, then fine-tune all layers
Skip training and use the ImageNet head directly
explain: Deployment shift is exactly where Kumar et al. found fine-tuning from a random head loses to probing, and where LP-FT won on 10 of 10 OOD datasets. The ImageNet head predicts ImageNet classes, and position embeddings alone cannot learn new classes.

courseTitle: Vision-language-action models: RT-2, OpenVLA and pi0
lessonTitle: Why per-step tokens break at 50 Hz, and how FAST compresses them
question: A bimanual robot (14 action dims) runs at 50 Hz. How many tokens does per-step 256-bin tokenization need for a 1-second chunk?
explain: 14 dims x 50 steps = 700 tokens, matching the FAST paper's shirt-folding row. FAST needed about 53 for the same chunk.

courseTitle: Visual tokenizers: turning images into discrete tokens
lessonTitle: Vector quantization: snap each vector to its nearest code
question: In the VQ-VAE loss, which parameters receive gradient from the middle term $\lVert \mathrm{sg}[z_e] - e \rVert^2$?
options: The encoder only
The decoder only
Both the encoder and the codebook
The codebook only
explain: sg blocks the gradient to z_e, so only the codebook vectors e are updated by this term. The paper states: the decoder optimises the first term, the encoder the first and last, and the embeddings the middle term.

courseTitle: Visual tokenizers: turning images into discrete tokens
lessonTitle: Token budgets: bits per image, 1D tokenizers and early fusion
question: You can either double the codebook from 8192 to 16,384 codes or halve the number of image tokens from 1024 to 512. Which choice reduces the stage 2 transformer's attention compute more, and why?
options: Doubling the codebook, because a larger softmax is the dominant cost
They are equivalent, since both change bits per image by the same factor
Halving tokens, because attention pairs scale with the square of sequence length while codebook size adds only one bit per token
Neither changes compute
explain: Halving T cuts attention pairs by 4x and bits per image by 2x. Doubling K adds 1 bit per token (13 to 14) and enlarges the embedding and output layers, but leaves sequence length, and thus attention cost, unchanged.

courseTitle: vLLM attention backends: selection, batching, KV layout, CUDA graphs
lessonTitle: Mixed prefill and decode in one forward pass
question: Request D has 32 of its 50 prompt tokens computed and runs 5 tokens; B is a fresh 6-token prompt; A, C and E decode 1 token each. Where does the runner's sort put D?
options: After the three decodes and before B, because the rest are ordered by query length (5 < 6)
With the decodes, since it already has context
At the very end, after B, because its prompt is unfinished
Nowhere special: FLASH_ATTN sets no threshold, so the batch is not sorted
explain: sort_batch_req_ids puts requests whose query length equals the decode length (1) first, then orders the rest by query length. Context does not enter the key, so D (5) precedes B (6); had B been a 3-token prompt, B would have come first. The sort runs for every backend.

courseTitle: vLLM attention backends: selection, batching, KV layout, CUDA graphs
lessonTitle: Hybrid models and KV cache groups: one pool, many block tables
question: Manager block size 128, a backend that runs 32-token kernel blocks, and a manager table [5, 2]. Which kernel block holds position 200?
options: Kernel block 10
Kernel block 6
Kernel block 22
explain: r = 128 / 32 = 4, so manager block 2 becomes kernel blocks 8 to 11. Position 200 is at table index 200 // 128 = 1 (block id 2), offset 72, and 72 // 32 = 2, so kernel block 2 x 4 + 2 = 10. Using the table index instead of the id gives 6; using block 5 gives 22; 328 is a slot-like number, not a block.

courseTitle: Vision-language models for reading images
lessonTitle: What an image costs: provider token formulas and resizing rules
question: Using Claude's formula, how many tokens does a 560 x 280 image cost (no resizing needed)?
explain: $\lceil 560/28 \rceil \cdot \lceil 280/28 \rceil = 20 \cdot 10 = 200$. 784 is $28^2$, and 156,800 is the raw pixel count.

courseTitle: Wait-free algorithms: bounded progress for every thread
lessonTitle: Herlihy's universal construction: announce, then help
question: A teammate removes the `help` lookup so each process always proposes its own cell. Which property is lost?
options: Linearizability: operations might be applied twice
Lock-freedom: the system might stop making progress
Wait-freedom: a slow process can lose every consensus round, though the system still progresses
Nothing: consensus still picks one cell per slot
explain: Each consensus round still threads exactly one cell, so the system progresses and nothing is applied twice. But nothing forces a slow process's cell to win, so that process can starve. Herlihy states this directly: without helping the protocol is non-blocking but not wait-free.

courseTitle: Weather and climate foundation models: GraphCast to Aurora
lessonTitle: Rolling a 6-hour step out to 10 days
question: Using Pangu-Weather's greedy schedule with 24, 6, 3 and 1 hour models, how many model calls produce a 100-hour forecast?
options: 6 calls: four 24 h, one 3 h, one 1 h
5 calls: four 24 h and one 4 h
17 calls: all 6 h steps
100 calls: all 1 h steps
explain: 100 = 4 x 24 + 4. The 6-hour model does not fit into the remaining 4 hours, so the greedy loop uses one 3-hour and one 1-hour call: 4 + 1 + 1 = 6. There is no 4-hour model.

courseTitle: Weather and climate foundation models: GraphCast to Aurora
lessonTitle: Foundation models, hybrids, and where these models break
question: A team has only 4 years of data for a new pollutant and wants global 5-day forecasts. Why is fine-tuning a pretrained Earth model like Aurora attractive?
options: The backbone already learned atmospheric dynamics from over a million hours of data, so only the new variables and mapping must be learned
Fine-tuning removes the need for any target data
Pretrained models do not need initial conditions
Fine-tuning guarantees beating CAMS on every target
explain: This is the foundation-model argument: the expensive dynamics are learned once. Aurora fine-tuned on limited CAMS analysis data (plus CAMS reanalysis) and matched or beat CAMS on 74% of targets, not all of them.

courseTitle: Web application testing and bug bounty practice
lessonTitle: Mapping the application: entry points, roles and workflows
question: A JavaScript bundle references /api/admin/refunds, which your normal test account never sees in the interface. What is the right next step?
options: Ignore it; hidden features are out of scope
Add it to the map and test whether a normal account can reach it, within the policy
Report it immediately as a vulnerability
Brute force admin credentials to reach it
explain: A route in client code is an entry point. Whether a normal user can call it is a function-level authorization test (WSTG-ATHZ-02). Its mere existence is not a vulnerability, and guessing admin passwords is outside any reasonable policy.

courseTitle: Web application testing and bug bounty practice
lessonTitle: Testing sessions: tokens, cookie flags, fixation and logout
question: An application uses stateless JWTs with a 30-day lifetime and no revocation. A user clicks 'log out' on a shared computer. What is the risk?
options: None, because the browser deleted the token
Anyone who copied the token earlier can use it for up to 30 days
The token becomes invalid immediately
Only the refresh token is affected
explain: Without server-side revocation, a self-contained token remains valid until it expires. Deleting the browser copy does not help if a copy was already taken.

courseTitle: Web application testing and bug bounty practice
lessonTitle: Chaining low findings into real impact
question: Why did Shopify pay the Exchange SSRF report as a core remote code execution, even though the screenshot service itself was minor?
options: Because all SSRF is paid at the maximum
Because the demonstrated chain reached containers in a subset with access to some core data and systems
Because the researcher asked for more
Because the report was public
explain: Shopify's summary says it awarded the report as a core RCE since some applications in that subset had access to core data. Rewards follow demonstrated, plausible end states linked to the root issue.

courseTitle: Web application testing and bug bounty practice
lessonTitle: Coordinated disclosure: when and how to publish
question: Under Project Zero's current Full 90 policy, a vendor ships a fix on day 20. When are the details published (assuming no exploitation in the wild and no vendor request)?
options: Day 20
Day 50
Day 90
Never
explain: Full X means publication X days after notification regardless of when the fix ships, so day 90. Earlier publication happens if the vendor requests it, if the bug is exploited in the wild (7 days) or if details become public elsewhere.

courseTitle: The browser security model
lessonTitle: Cookies, sessions, and how Firesheep hijacked them in 2010
question: A developer proposes encrypting the session cookie's value with a server key as the fix for sidejacking. Why is that not enough?
options: The attacker can still copy the whole encrypted cookie and replay it; the server will accept it
Encryption makes the cookie too long for browsers
Browsers reject encrypted cookies
It is enough; an encrypted cookie cannot be used by anyone else
explain: The server only checks that the cookie it receives is valid. A stolen encrypted cookie is still valid. The fix is to keep the cookie off the network in clear text (HTTPS everywhere plus Secure) and to revoke sessions on suspicion.

courseTitle: The browser security model
lessonTitle: Content Security Policy: telling the browser which scripts to trust
question: A page sends `Content-Security-Policy: script-src 'nonce-abc123' 'unsafe-inline'`. An attacker injects `<script>steal()</script>` with no nonce. What happens?
options: It runs only in report-only mode
It is blocked, because 'unsafe-inline' is ignored when the directive contains a nonce
The whole policy is invalid and ignored
It runs, because 'unsafe-inline' allows inline scripts
explain: When a nonce or hash is present in the directive, supporting browsers ignore 'unsafe-inline'. The injected script lacks the nonce, so it is blocked. Old browsers that do not understand nonces fall back to 'unsafe-inline', which is why sites sometimes list both.

courseTitle: The browser security model
lessonTitle: Subresource Integrity and the trust you hand to third-party scripts
question: A script tag has `integrity="sha256-AAA... sha384-BBB..."`. The file's SHA-256 matches AAA but its SHA-384 does not match BBB. What does the browser do?
options: Refuses it: only the strongest algorithm listed (SHA-384) is checked, and it does not match
Runs it with a console warning
Asks the user
Runs it, because one hash matched
explain: MDN: the browser selects the hashes made with the strongest function present and ignores weaker ones. Only sha384-BBB is compared, it fails, and the script is not executed.

courseTitle: Windows for security: accounts, processes, registry and event logs
lessonTitle: The map: what happens when you open one file on Windows
question: Which attacker goal does clearing the Security event log serve?
options: Getting in
Climbing to administrator
Hiding
Moving to other machines
explain: Clearing logs removes evidence. Windows records a separate event (1102) when the Security log is cleared, which you will meet in the event log lessons.

courseTitle: Windows for security: accounts, processes, registry and event logs
lessonTitle: UAC and integrity levels: why admins do not run as admin
question: A low-integrity browser process tries to modify a file in Ana's Documents folder. The file's DACL allows Ana full control. What happens?
options: Allowed, because the DACL allows Ana
Allowed only after a UAC prompt
Blocked, because the integrity check runs before the DACL and forbids writing up to medium
Blocked, because browsers have no token
explain: Mandatory Integrity Control is evaluated before the DACL. A low-integrity token cannot write to a medium (or unlabeled) object, whatever the DACL says.

courseTitle: Windows for security: accounts, processes, registry and event logs
lessonTitle: The registry, Run keys and scheduled tasks: how programs come back
question: You want an alert whenever anyone creates a scheduled task on servers. What must be true for event 4698 to appear?
options: Nothing; 4698 is always on
Sysmon must be installed
The audit policy must enable the Audit Other Object Access Events subcategory
The task must run as SYSTEM
explain: 4698 belongs to the Audit Other Object Access Events subcategory. If that auditing is off, the Security log stays silent when tasks are created.

courseTitle: Windows for security: accounts, processes, registry and event logs
lessonTitle: SMB file shares and EternalBlue: how WannaCry spread
question: According to the NAO, what would have protected NHS organisations from WannaCry even if they had not patched?
options: Paying the ransom quickly
Renaming the Administrator account
Managing their internet-facing firewalls
Turning on script block logging
explain: The NAO report says that whether or not systems were patched, managing internet-facing firewalls would have guarded organisations against infection. Reachability matters as much as the bug.

courseTitle: Wireless and mobile security
lessonTitle: Why wireless is different: a medium anyone in range can hear
question: Your office network hides its SSID and allows only a list of known MAC addresses. A visitor in the car park runs a laptop in monitor mode. What do these two controls stop?
options: Both stop the visitor from joining, because the SSID is secret
Neither: the SSID appears in management frames from legitimate clients and permitted MAC addresses travel in the clear, ready to be copied
MAC filtering stops them, hiding the SSID does not
They stop eavesdropping but not joining
explain: Arbaugh and colleagues showed both fail against a passive listener: clients reveal the SSID when they associate, and every frame carries source MAC addresses unencrypted. Use real authentication (WPA3 or 802.1X) instead.

courseTitle: Wireless and mobile security
lessonTitle: WPA2-Enterprise: 802.1X, EAP and the certificate check that matters
question: A company uses PEAP-MSCHAPv2. Laptops trust the operating system's whole CA store and have no server name configured. What can an attacker with a public certificate for their own domain do?
options: Stand up an AP with the company SSID and receive users' MSCHAPv2 exchanges inside a tunnel that ends at the attacker
Decrypt the company's past traffic
Only cause a denial of service
Nothing; PEAP encrypts everything
explain: The client accepts any certificate chaining to a trusted CA, so the TLS tunnel happily terminates at the attacker. NIST SP 800-97 describes this exact scenario and its fix: a specific CA plus a server name check.

courseTitle: Wireless and mobile security
lessonTitle: Rogue access points, evil twins and how enterprises find them
question: An employee plugs a cheap travel router into their desk port to get better Wi-Fi, with its own SSID 'Jo-Hotspot' and WPA2-PSK. Which control would have stopped this from opening a path into the LAN?
options: Hiding the CorpNet SSID
OWE on the guest network
WPA3 on the corporate APs
802.1X on the wired access port, so an unauthenticated device gets no network access
explain: The rogue AP's risk is on the wired side: it bridges radio clients onto your LAN. Port-based authentication blocks unknown devices at the switch. WIDS would detect it; 802.1X prevents it.

courseTitle: Wireless and mobile security
lessonTitle: Android: UID sandbox, SELinux, verified boot and Play Protect
question: Why does verified boot include rollback protection?
options: To make updates faster
So that an attacker cannot reinstall an older, signed but vulnerable system image to exploit a bug that has since been fixed
To roll back bad updates automatically
To protect the user's photos
explain: Old images were validly signed too. Without rollback protection, signing alone would let an attacker downgrade to a version with a known exploit and make it persistent.

courseTitle: Wireless and mobile security
lessonTitle: Managing fleets: MDM, BYOD and SIM swap defences
question: A help-desk policy lets users reset their VPN password with a code sent by SMS. Which attack does this expose, regardless of how well the phone itself is managed?
options: A SIM swap that diverts the SMS code to the attacker's SIM
BlueBorne
An evil twin
KRACK
explain: The attacker attacks the carrier, not the device: once the number moves, codes go to them. The FBI PSA describes exactly this use against account recovery. Move recovery to non-SMS factors.

courseTitle: Work stealing and thread pools
lessonTitle: Owner pops newest, thief steals oldest: why the ends matter
question: A worker's deque holds, from top to bottom, tasks of 40, 20, 10 and 5 units pushed by one recursive split. A thief steals once and the owner pops once. Which tasks do they get?
options: Thief 5, owner 40
Thief 40, owner 5
Thief 40, owner 20
Both race for 5
explain: Thieves take from the top, where the oldest and here largest task (40) sits. The owner pops the bottom, the newest (5). They only contend when exactly one task is left.

courseTitle: Work stealing and thread pools
lessonTitle: Parking idle workers without lost wakeups or thundering herds
question: Which change to the giving-up path reintroduces lost wakeups?
options: Removing the barrier between decrementing the searcher count and rechecking the queues
Starting the search at a random victim
Stealing half instead of one task
Capping searchers at half the workers
explain: The barrier makes the searcher's decrement visible before it rereads the queues, so a concurrent submitter either sees zero searchers (and wakes someone) or its task is seen by the recheck. The other choices affect efficiency, not correctness.

courseTitle: WSD learning-rate schedules
lessonTitle: Run it yourself: one stable trunk, three cooldown branches
question: A cooldown branch shows a sharp loss jump on its very first step and then slowly recovers. The LR log shows the expected 1-sqrt decay from the peak. What was most likely left out of the restore?
options: The AdamW state (its moments and step count)
The data loader position
The model weights
The validation set
explain: With fresh moments, Adam's bias-corrected first update is about the LR times the sign of the gradient for every weight, a large uniform step. Missing weights would start from random init (a huge loss), and a wrong data position changes which batches are seen but does not cause a first-step jump.

courseTitle: Zero-copy I/O: sendfile, splice and MSG_ZEROCOPY
lessonTitle: sendfile: from the page cache straight to the socket
question: Your proxy receives bytes on one TCP socket and forwards them to another. A teammate suggests `sendfile(out_sock, in_sock, NULL, n)`. What happens?
options: It works and is zero-copy end to end
It fails, because in_fd must support mmap-like operations and a socket does not
It works but copies through user space
It fails, because out_fd may not be a socket
explain: sendfile reads from something with page-cache-like pages, a regular file. A socket is not that, so the call fails with EINVAL. Forwarding between sockets needs splice with a pipe in the middle (lesson 3). out_fd being a socket is the classic use case, so the last option is wrong.

courseTitle: Zero-shot classification: labels chosen at inference time
lessonTitle: Classifying with labels chosen at inference time
question: CLIP averages 80 prompt embeddings per class instead of averaging 80 sets of predicted probabilities. What does that buy at inference time?
options: Higher accuracy, because averaging probabilities is mathematically invalid
It removes the need for a temperature parameter
The ensemble costs the same as one prompt: one cached text vector per class, one image encoding per input
It lets CLIP output several labels per image
explain: Averaging in embedding space collapses the 80 prompts into one vector per class ahead of time. At inference, each image is still compared with exactly one vector per class, so the ensemble is free once the averages are cached. The paper gives exactly this reason.
